section.title: The Peace Offering
section.sectionRationale: The third of the five offerings, the peace offering is the only one of the major sacrifices that the worshiper himself gets to eat, shared in a meal before the LORD. It continues the sacrificial law collection, showing that atonement leads not only to acceptance but to fellowship.
section.thesis: The peace offering, whether from the herd, the flock, or a goat, gives all the fat to God on the altar while the meat becomes a shared meal, teaching that reconciliation with God issues in genuine fellowship and celebration in His presence.
section.frameNote: Three movements, one for each kind of animal, herd, sheep, and goat, each ending in the same refrain: all the fat belongs to the LORD.

units.label: An animal from the herd
units.note: hands laid on the head, blood sprinkled

verses.text: “If one's offering is a {{shelamim|peace offering}} and he offers an animal from the herd, whether male or female, he must present it without blemish before the LORD.
He is to lay his hand on the head of the offering and slaughter it at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting. Then Aaron's sons the priests shall sprinkle the blood on all sides of the altar.
From the peace offering he is to bring an offering made by fire to the LORD: the {{chelev|fat}} that covers the entrails, all the fat that is on them,
both kidneys with the fat on them near the loins, and the lobe of the liver, which he is to remove with the kidneys.
Then Aaron's sons are to burn it on the altar atop the burnt offering that is on the burning wood, as an offering made by fire, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
If, however, one's peace offering to the LORD is from the flock, he must present a male or female without blemish.
If he is presenting a lamb for his offering, he must present it before the LORD.
He is to lay his hand on the head of his offering and slaughter it in front of the Tent of Meeting. Then Aaron's sons shall sprinkle its blood on all sides of the altar.

And from the peace offering he shall bring an offering made by fire to the LORD consisting of its fat: the entire fat tail cut off close to the backbone, the fat that covers the entrails, all the fat that is on them,
both kidneys with the fat on them near the loins, and the lobe of the liver, which he is to remove with the kidneys.
Then the priest is to burn them on the altar as food, an offering made by fire to the LORD.

units.label: A goat
units.note: the same pattern, a permanent statute

verses.text: If one's offering is a goat, he is to present it before the LORD.
He must lay his hand on its head and slaughter it in front of the Tent of Meeting. Then Aaron's sons shall sprinkle its blood on all sides of the altar.
And from his offering he shall present an offering made by fire to the LORD: the fat that covers the entrails, all the fat that is on them,
both kidneys with the fat on them near the loins, and the lobe of the liver, which he is to remove with the kidneys.
Then the priest is to burn the food on the altar as an offering made by fire, a pleasing aroma. All the fat is the LORD's.
This is a permanent statute for the generations to come, wherever you live: You must not eat any fat or any blood.”

shelamim.gloss: The peace offering, related to shalom, wholeness or well being. Unlike the burnt offering, the worshiper shares in eating this sacrifice, so it pictures a completed, restored relationship celebrated in a shared meal before God.

chelev.gloss: Fat, considered the richest and best part of the animal. Reserved exclusively for God and never to be eaten, verse 17, the fat represents giving the LORD the finest portion before anything is kept back for human use.

basic.context: The peace offering is the third of the five great sacrifices, and it stands apart because the worshiper actually eats most of the meat, sharing a celebratory meal in God's presence. Whatever the animal, an ox, a lamb, or a goat, the fat and inner organs always belong entirely to the LORD, burned on the altar, while the meat becomes food for a shared meal.
basic.hermeneutics: This describes Israel's actual old covenant sacrificial system, not a ritual for Christians to repeat today. Its abiding truth is that peace with God, once atonement is made, leads to genuine fellowship, joy, and shared celebration rather than mere formal acceptance.
basic.originalLanguages: Shelamim is related to shalom, meaning wholeness and well being, showing that this offering pictures a relationship restored to completeness. Chelev, fat, the richest part of the animal, always belongs to God alone, teaching that the best portion is reserved for Him before anything is kept for human enjoyment.
basic.typology: The shared meal, where the worshiper eats in God's presence, anticipates the fellowship believers now enjoy with God through Christ and looks forward to the marriage supper of the Lamb. The exclusive claim on the fat, the richest part, foreshadows giving God the very best rather than mere leftovers.
basic.christ: Christ is our peace, Ephesians 2:14, who has made peace through the blood of His cross, Colossians 1:20, and who now invites His people to feast with Him, both now at His table and finally at the marriage supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9.
basic.god: God does not merely tolerate sinners at a distance once atonement is made; He invites them to a shared meal in His presence, revealing His desire for genuine fellowship, not just formal reconciliation. His claim on the fat, the best part, shows He is not satisfied with token or leftover devotion.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 2:14 calls Christ our peace. Colossians 1:20 says God made peace through the blood of Christ's cross. Revelation 19:9 describes the marriage supper of the Lamb, the ultimate shared feast with God.
basic.oneStory: The peace offering shows that atonement is not the end of the story but the beginning of fellowship, a shared meal celebrating restored relationship with God. That pattern anticipates Christ, who is Himself our peace, and who invites His reconciled people to feast with Him now and forever at His table.

context.literary:
Leviticus 3 is built with the same care as chapter 1 but on a tighter plan. There are three cases, the herd, verses 1 to 5, the flock as a lamb, verses 6 to 11, and the goat, verses 12 to 16, and each moves through the same steps: present the animal, lay the hand, slaughter at the tent, sprinkle the blood, remove the fat and burn it. The lists of fat in verses 3 to 4, 9 to 10 and 14 to 15 are nearly identical, word for word, so that the repetition itself becomes the lesson. Whatever the animal, the same parts go to God.

The chapter's ending gathers everything into two sentences. 'All the fat is the LORD's,' verse 16, and 'You must not eat any fat or any blood,' verse 17. The first states the principle, the second turns it into a law for daily life 'wherever you live.' A chapter about the altar ends by reaching into every Israelite home.

Placement matters. The peace offering follows the burnt offering and the grain offering, and it is burned 'atop the burnt offering that is on the burning wood,' verse 5, as though laid on the foundation the first offering provides. Chapters 1 to 3 describe offerings that a worshiper might bring freely, each closing with 'a pleasing aroma,' before chapters 4 and 5 turn to offerings required for sin. The fuller instructions for the peace offering, including the meal itself, are held back until Leviticus 7:11-36, where the priests learn what they eat and when.

The most striking literary feature is what the chapter does not say. It never describes the meal. Chapter 3 tells only God's part, the blood and the fat. The reader must wait for chapter 7 to learn that the rest is eaten, and that absence focuses attention on God's portion first. The meal comes only after the LORD has received what is His.
context.historical:
For most Israelites, meat was not an everyday food. Flocks and herds were wealth, kept for milk, wool and breeding, and slaughter was an occasion. The peace offering was therefore the great feast of Israel's life, the time when a family ate meat together in God's presence. Leviticus 17:3-5 required that, while Israel lived in the camp, any ox, lamb or goat slaughtered be brought to the tent as a peace offering. When the people later spread across the land, Deuteronomy 12:15-16 allowed ordinary slaughter at home, but still not the eating of blood.

The meal had rules of its own. A thanksgiving offering had to be eaten the same day; a vow or freewill offering could be eaten the next day, but anything left until the third day had to be burned, Leviticus 7:15-17. Anyone ceremonially unclean who ate it would be cut off, Leviticus 7:20. The priest received the breast, waved before the LORD, and the right thigh, Leviticus 7:30-34. The rest was the worshiper's to share. Deuteronomy pictures whole households eating with their servants and the Levite, rejoicing before the LORD, Deuteronomy 12:18. Elkanah gave portions to his whole family at Shiloh, 1 Samuel 1:4-5.

The fat of verses 3 and 4 is the suet, the firm fat around the entrails and kidneys, not the fat marbled through the meat. The 'entire fat tail' of verse 9 belongs to the broad-tailed sheep of the region, whose tail could be large and heavy.

The chapter also distanced Israel from surrounding practice. Ezekiel describes the king of Babylon who 'examines the liver' to seek an omen, Ezekiel 21:21, reflecting the widespread art of reading livers. In Israel the lobe of the liver was not read; it was removed and burned for God, verses 4, 10 and 15. And Leviticus 17:7 says the peace offerings at the tent replaced sacrifices once made in the open fields 'to the goat demons.'

Abuse of the rule could become notorious. At Shiloh the sons of Eli demanded meat 'even before the fat was burned,' 1 Samuel 2:15-17, treating the LORD's offering with contempt.
context.canonical:
The peace offering first appears at the covenant meal of Sinai. Young men 'sacrificed young bulls as peace offerings,' Exodus 24:5, and the elders of Israel 'saw Him, and they ate and drank,' Exodus 24:11. It is the offering of covenant fellowship from the beginning. Earlier still, Jacob 'offered a sacrifice on the mountain and invited his relatives to eat a meal,' Genesis 31:54, sealing a covenant with Laban.

Throughout Israel's history the peace offering marks moments of joy and dedication. David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings when the ark came to Jerusalem and then gave food to the whole multitude, 2 Samuel 6:17-19. Solomon dedicated the temple with 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep as peace offerings, 1 Kings 8:63. The people also offered peace offerings while weeping and fasting at Bethel, Judges 20:26, which shows that fellowship with God was sought in distress as well as in celebration. The Psalms echo the thanksgiving meal: 'I will offer to You a sacrifice of thanksgiving... I will fulfill my vows to the LORD in the presence of all His people,' Psalm 116:17-18, and 'The poor will eat and be satisfied,' Psalm 22:26. Proverbs 7:14 shows the offering corrupted, as the adulteress uses the meat of her peace offerings as an invitation to sin.

The prophets look ahead to a greater feast. 'On this mountain the LORD of Hosts will prepare a banquet for all the peoples, a feast of aged wine, of choice meat,' Isaiah 25:6. The fat of verse 16 belongs to God, and in Isaiah God Himself sets the richest food before the nations.

The New Testament picks up both the meal and the prohibition. Paul asks, 'Are not those who eat the sacrifices fellow partakers in the altar?' 1 Corinthians 10:18, and compares the Lord's Supper to that sharing, 1 Corinthians 10:16-17. Hebrews says, 'We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat,' Hebrews 13:10. The Jerusalem council asks Gentile believers to abstain 'from blood,' Acts 15:20, recalling verse 17 and Genesis 9:4. And the father of the prodigal says, 'Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let us feast and celebrate,' Luke 15:23, the joy of the peace offering in a story of reconciliation.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to understand that the goal of approaching God is fellowship. The burnt offering went wholly up to God; the peace offering ends at a table. The worshiper who had drawn near through blood could eat in God's presence and share the joy with his household and the poor.

He wanted them to see that fellowship still rests on atonement. The laying on of the hand and the sprinkling of blood come first in every case, verses 2, 8 and 13. The meal does not replace the altar; it follows it.

He also wanted Israel to learn an order of honour. God's portion, the fat and the organs, comes off first and is burned before anyone eats. The rule 'all the fat is the LORD's,' verse 16, taught Israel that the best belongs to Him, not as a tax that spoils the feast but as the grace that makes the feast possible.

And he wanted the lesson to reach every home. Verse 17 turns an altar rule into a daily one, 'wherever you live.' Every meal of meat would remind an Israelite that life belongs to God and that the best was His.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Leviticus 3 prescribes a sacrifice for Israel's sanctuary, and its details were tied to the tabernacle and priesthood that Christ has fulfilled. Christians do not bring peace offerings, and they are not bound to the food laws of this chapter. Mark notes that Jesus' teaching made 'all foods clean,' Mark 7:19, and Paul warns, 'let no one judge you by what you eat or drink,' because these things were 'a shadow of the things to come,' Colossians 2:16-17.

The ban on blood is more complex. It is older than Sinai, given to Noah, Genesis 9:4, and the Jerusalem council asked Gentile believers to abstain from blood, Acts 15:20 and 15:29. Christians have differed on whether that request was a lasting command or a practical step to protect fellowship between Jewish and Gentile believers, a point discussed below.

What clearly carries over is the shape of the offering. Fellowship with God follows reconciliation through blood, Colossians 1:20. God's people eat together in His presence, now at the Lord's Table, 1 Corinthians 10:16-17. They give God the first and best, not what is left. And they share their joy with others, as the peace offering fed household, servants, Levite and poor.

debates.question: What does the name shelamim mean, and what kind of offering is it?

views.label: A peace offering, celebrating peace with God
views.case: The word shares its root with shalom, and the offering follows atonement and ends in a meal. Many English versions translate 'peace offering' on that basis, stressing the restored relationship between God and the worshiper.

views.label: A fellowship offering, stressing the shared meal
views.case: Others prefer 'fellowship offering,' as some modern versions do, because the offering's distinctive feature is that God, priest and worshiper each receive a portion. Paul's comment that those who eat the sacrifices are 'fellow partakers in the altar,' 1 Corinthians 10:18, supports this emphasis.

views.label: An offering of well-being or payment
views.case: A third view connects the name with the related verb shillem, to pay or fulfil, since the peace offering was often brought 'to fulfill a vow,' Leviticus 22:21. Proverbs 7:14 pairs 'I have made my peace offerings' with 'I have paid my vows,' using both words together.

debates.bearing: Each view catches something real. The offering expresses wholeness with God, it is shared at a meal, and it often fulfilled a vow or gave thanks. Its three kinds in Leviticus 7:11-16, thanksgiving, vow and freewill, show that all three ideas belong to it.

debates.question: Does the prohibition of fat and blood in verse 17 bind Christians?

views.label: No, it was part of the ceremonial law fulfilled in Christ
views.case: The fat was forbidden because it belonged to the altar, Leviticus 7:25, and the altar has been fulfilled. Jesus declared all foods clean, Mark 7:19, and Paul treats food laws as a shadow, Colossians 2:16-17. On this view Acts 15:20 was a practical request for mixed churches so that Gentile believers would not offend Jewish neighbours.

views.label: The blood prohibition continues, though the fat law does not
views.case: Others distinguish the two. The fat law is tied to the sanctuary, but the blood law was given to Noah for all humanity, Genesis 9:4, before Israel existed, and the council repeated it for Gentiles as seeming 'good to the Holy Spirit,' Acts 15:28-29. On this view respect for blood as the sign of life still belongs to believers.

debates.bearing: Most of the church has concluded that the fat law has ended with the altar it served. On blood, the consistent point is reverence for life, which belongs to God. Whatever one concludes about diet, verse 17 should teach believers that life is not ours to treat casually.

study.originalLanguages:
The full name in verse 1 is zevach shelamim, 'a sacrifice of peace offering.' Zevach comes from the verb zavach, to slaughter for sacrifice, the same root as mizbeach, 'altar,' the place of slaughter. In the offerings a zevach is usually a sacrifice that ends in a meal, as opposed to the olah that goes wholly up in smoke.

Shelamim is plural, and its root sh-l-m carries a range of ideas: shalom, peace and well-being; shalem, whole or complete; and shillem, to pay or fulfil. The range explains why translations vary between 'peace offering' and 'fellowship offering,' and why the offering is so often linked to vows. Proverbs 7:14 puts two forms of the root side by side: 'I have made my peace offerings; today I have paid my vows.'

The fat is chelev. The word names the suet of the animal, but it is also used for the best of anything. Abel brought 'the best portions of the firstborn of his flock,' Genesis 4:4, literally their fat. Pharaoh promises Joseph's family 'the fat of the land,' Genesis 45:18. God says He would feed His people 'the finest wheat,' Psalm 81:16, and Numbers 18:12 gives the priests 'the freshest olive oil,' each time using chelev for the best. David says, 'My soul is satisfied as with the richest of foods,' Psalm 63:5, where the Hebrew speaks of fat and richness. When verse 16 says 'All the fat is the LORD's,' it means the best is His.

Kelayot, the kidneys of verses 4, 10 and 15, is also used for the inner self. 'I, the LORD, search the heart; I examine the mind,' Jeremiah 17:10, uses kelayot for 'mind,' and Psalm 7:9 speaks of God 'who searches hearts and minds' with the same word. The organs of the inner body, hidden from sight, are the ones given to God.

The 'lobe of the liver,' yoteret, is literally the appendage or what projects from the liver. Its exact identification is uncertain, but it is always removed with the kidneys, and the same list appears for the ordination ram, Exodus 29:13, and for the sin offering, Leviticus 4:8-10, which says the fat is removed 'just as the fat is removed from the ox of the peace offering.'

Verses 11 and 16 call the burned portion 'food,' lechem, the common word for bread or food. Leviticus 21:6 calls the offerings 'the food of their God,' and Numbers 28:2 speaks of 'the food for My offerings by fire.' The language is covenant language: God shares the meal. Psalm 50:12-13 makes sure no one thinks He is hungry.

Verse 17 calls the rule a 'permanent statute,' chuqqat olam, for the generations 'wherever you live,' extending an altar law into every dwelling.

typology.type: The shared meal after the blood is applied
typology.fulfillment: In the peace offering God, priest and worshiper all receive a portion, and the meal follows the altar. Jesus took bread and a cup and said, 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood,' Luke 22:20, and Paul says the bread and cup are 'a participation in the body' and 'the blood of Christ,' comparing it to Israel eating the sacrifices, 1 Corinthians 10:16-18. The escalation is that believers now feed on Christ Himself, John 6:56. The type falls short because the meat had to be eaten within two days and then burned; the fellowship Christ gives lasts forever.

The meal of the peace offering was possible only after blood was sprinkled on the altar, verses 2, 8 and 13. Paul says God reconciled all things to Himself 'by making peace through the blood of His cross,' Colossians 1:20, and that 'He Himself is our peace,' Ephesians 2:14. The escalation is that Christ is not only the sacrifice that makes peace but the peace itself, and He joins Jew and Gentile at one table. The type falls short because each animal made peace for one worshiper for a moment; Christ's blood reconciles a people permanently.

typology.type: The fattened calf and the feast of reconciliation
typology.fulfillment: The father of the prodigal says, 'Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let us feast and celebrate,' Luke 15:23. The feast has the shape of a peace offering: a slaughtered animal, a family meal and joy at restored relationship. Jesus uses it to show God's heart toward sinners who return. The escalation is that heaven itself rejoices, Luke 15:7. The type falls short in that the parable does not mention an altar, reminding us that the father's welcome is free, though the New Testament shows elsewhere what it cost.

typology.type: The fat reserved for God and the banquet God prepares
typology.fulfillment: In Leviticus 3 the best portion goes up to God and the worshiper eats the rest. In Isaiah 25:6 God Himself prepares 'a banquet for all the peoples... of choice meat,' and Revelation 19:9 blesses 'those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.' The escalation is a reversal: the God who once received the fat now sets the richest food before His guests. The type falls short because the peace offering was limited to Israel and to a day, while the final feast gathers every nation for all time.

study.christ:
The peace offering leads to Christ first through His own words about peace. The prophet had called the coming king 'Prince of Peace,' Isaiah 9:6, and said, 'the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him,' Isaiah 53:5. Jesus told His disciples, 'Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you,' John 14:27. Paul then speaks in the language of the altar: 'Since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,' Romans 5:1, and God made 'peace through the blood of His cross,' Colossians 1:20. The order of Leviticus 3, blood first and then the meal, is the order of the gospel.

It leads to Christ through the meal. At the Last Supper Jesus took bread and a cup and said, 'This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins,' Matthew 26:28. The disciples ate and drank what He called His body and blood. Paul explains the Supper by comparing it to Israel's sacrificial meals: 'Are not those who eat the sacrifices fellow partakers in the altar?' 1 Corinthians 10:18. The Lord's Supper is not a new sacrifice, but it is a meal that feeds on the one sacrifice, as the peace offering fed on an animal already offered.

It leads to Christ through His table fellowship. Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners, told the story of the fattened calf, Luke 15:23, and after His resurrection was recognized 'in the breaking of the bread,' Luke 24:35. Revelation 3:20 has Him say, 'I will come in and dine with him, and he with Me.' The worshiper who once ate before the LORD at the tent now eats with the Lord Himself.

Hebrews adds a sharp contrast. 'We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat,' Hebrews 13:10. The peace offering's meat was eaten by clean Israelites at the tent; the Christian's feast is on Christ, who 'suffered outside the city gate,' Hebrews 13:12, and those who cling to the old system cannot share it.

The fat reserved for God also points to Christ, though more gently. Everything best in the animal went to God. In Christ the Father received the whole of His Son's obedience, and the Son gave Himself as the choicest offering. We should not press every organ in the list for meaning; the New Testament does not. The link lies in the pattern of the offering as a whole: blood that reconciles, a portion that honours God, and a meal that celebrates restored fellowship. Christ fulfils all three, and He will drink the fruit of the vine anew with His people in His Father's kingdom, Matthew 26:29.
study.god:
The peace offering shows a God who eats with His people. The language is bold: the burned portion is 'food,' verses 11 and 16, 'the food of their God,' Leviticus 21:6. Psalm 50:12-13 rules out any idea that God is hungry, so the language is relational. The God of Israel sets a table and shares it. He does not merely forgive sinners at a distance; He invites them to feast.

He is the God who comes first. Every case in the chapter puts God's portion before the meal. The fat, the kidneys and the lobe of the liver are removed and burned before anyone else eats. The rule 'All the fat is the LORD's,' verse 16, is not greed; it is a confession that everything good comes from Him and that He is worthy of the best. Eli's sons, who took their meat before the fat was burned, were 'treating the LORD's offering with contempt,' 1 Samuel 2:17.

He is holy in fellowship. The meal had strict rules: eaten within a day or two, only by the clean, Leviticus 7:15-21. God's nearness does not make Him casual. Joy and reverence belong together at His table.

He is generous. The peace offering was usually voluntary, for thanksgiving, a vow, or simply a freewill gift, Leviticus 7:11-16. God gave His people a way to express gratitude and to celebrate, and He built into the offering a meal that could be shared with servants, Levites and the poor, Deuteronomy 12:18. His worship is not joyless.

He is the Lord of life. Verse 17 forbids blood in every home, and Leviticus 17:11 explains why: 'the life of the flesh is in the blood.' God claims all life as His. The law of blood taught Israel that even their daily meals rested on His gift of life and His provision for atonement.

He searches the inner person. The kidneys, whose Hebrew name stands for the inner self when God 'examines the mind,' Jeremiah 17:10, are among the parts given to God. What is hidden belongs to Him.

For worship, the chapter calls believers to come to God's table with thanks, with reverence, and with open hands for others. It also reminds us that the peace we enjoy is costly and that God receives the first place in all our joys. He who received the fat of Israel's offerings now invites the nations to a banquet of His own, Isaiah 25:6.

crossReferences.note: At the covenant ceremony young men offered peace offerings, and the elders of Israel saw God 'and they ate and drank.' The peace offering begins as the meal of covenant fellowship, the pattern Leviticus 3 institutes for every worshiper.

The law of the peace offering fills in what chapter 3 leaves out. It names three kinds, thanksgiving, vow and freewill, sets the time limits for eating the meat, and forbids anyone unclean to eat it. It shows the joy of the meal held within God's holiness.

The priest receives the breast, waved before the LORD, and the right thigh. The worshiper must bring the fat 'with his own hands.' Together with Leviticus 3, it shows how the peace offering was divided among God, priest and worshiper.

The reason for the blood prohibition of Leviticus 3:17: 'the life of the flesh is in the blood,' and God has given it to make atonement on the altar. Blood is withheld from the table because it belongs to God for the covering of sin.

Eli's sons demanded meat before the fat was burned and threatened to take it by force. The narrator calls their sin severe, for they treated the LORD's offering with contempt. The episode shows why 'All the fat is the LORD's' mattered.

The psalmist promises a sacrifice of thanksgiving and to fulfil his vows in the presence of all God's people. These are two of the occasions for a peace offering, Leviticus 7:12-16, and the psalm shows the public joy they expressed.

The LORD will prepare on His mountain a banquet of choice meat and aged wine for all peoples. The meal of the peace offering, once limited to Israel's tent, becomes a vision of God feasting with the nations.

The father welcomes his lost son with the fattened calf, a feast and celebration because the son 'was dead and is alive again.' Jesus paints God's welcome of sinners in the colours of the peace offering, with joy that follows reconciliation.

Paul explains the Lord's Supper as participation in Christ's body and blood and compares it to Israel's sacrificial meals, where those who eat 'are fellow partakers in the altar.' The peace offering's shared meal becomes the model for the church's table.

God reconciled all things to Himself by making peace through the blood of Christ's cross. Leviticus 3 required blood before the meal; the gospel likewise grounds fellowship with God on the blood of the one sacrifice.

Christ Himself is our peace. He tore down the dividing wall and reconciled Jew and Gentile to God in one body through the cross. The peace offering celebrated peace with God; in Christ that peace also unites former enemies at one table.

The angel pronounces blessed 'those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.' The final feast of Scripture completes the pattern of the peace offering: a sacrifice made, a covenant sealed, and God's people eating with Him in joy.

study.oneStory:
In the garden God gave the man and woman food to eat in His presence. The fall broke that fellowship, and outside Eden bread would come 'by the sweat of your brow,' Genesis 3:19. The peace offering is part of God's answer. It restores, in picture, the meal in God's presence that sin had lost.

It answers what came before in Exodus. At Sinai the elders ate and drank before God after peace offerings were made, Exodus 24:11. Leviticus 3 makes that covenant meal available to ordinary Israelites, on the herd, the flock or a goat. It builds on the burnt offering, laid 'atop' it, verse 5, because fellowship rests on atonement.

It sets up what follows. The peace offering marks the joy of Israel's history, the ark coming to Jerusalem and the dedication of the temple. It also shows how that joy can be abused, as at Shiloh. The prophets look beyond Israel's tent to a banquet for all nations on God's mountain, Isaiah 25:6.

The story turns in Christ. He is our peace, and He made peace by the blood of His cross. On the night He was betrayed He gave His disciples bread and a cup and called them His body and blood of the covenant. The church now eats at His table, sharing in the one sacrifice, and Jews and Gentiles sit together because the dividing wall is gone, Ephesians 2:14.

The story ends at a feast. 'Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb,' Revelation 19:9. There God's people will eat with Him without time limits, without uncleanness and without end. The fat that once went up in smoke for God will be answered by the choice food God Himself sets before His guests, and the peace of the peace offering will be the lasting shalom of the new creation.

quiz.q: What distinguishes the peace offering from the burnt offering?

options.text: Most of the meat becomes food for a shared meal, rather than being wholly burned.
options.note: Only the fat and inner organs are burned, verses 3 to 5; the rest becomes a shared meal, unlike the burnt offering which is wholly consumed.

options.text: No blood is applied to the altar.
options.note: Verses 2, 8, and 13 all specify that blood is sprinkled on all sides of the altar, just as with the burnt offering.

options.text: It can only be offered by priests.
options.note: The chapter describes any Israelite worshiper bringing this offering, not only priests.

options.text: There is no meaningful difference.
options.note: The shared meal is the distinguishing feature that sets this offering apart from the burnt offering.

quiz.q: What three animals from the herd, flock, and beyond does this chapter permit for the peace offering?

options.text: An animal from the herd, a lamb from the flock, and a goat.
options.note: The three sections of the chapter, verses 1, 6 to 7, and 12, describe exactly these three categories.

options.text: Only doves and pigeons.
options.note: Birds are permitted for the burnt and sin offerings for the poor, but this chapter describes herd, flock, and goat animals.

options.text: Only bulls.
options.note: The chapter describes more than bulls alone, including lambs and goats.

options.text: No animals are specified.
options.note: The chapter gives detailed specifications for three categories of animals.

quiz.q: What part of the peace offering is always burned on the altar and never eaten by anyone?

options.text: The fat, including the fat covering the entrails and around the kidneys and liver.
options.note: Verses 3 to 4, 9 to 10, and 14 to 16 all specify this fat as belonging entirely to the LORD.

options.text: The meat of the shoulder.
options.note: The shoulder is not the portion specified here as reserved for the altar; the fat is.

options.text: The skin and hide.
options.note: The chapter concerns the fat portions, not the hide.

options.text: Nothing is reserved; the whole animal is eaten.
options.note: Verse 16 explicitly states that all the fat belongs to the LORD.

quiz.q: What permanent statute closes this chapter, verse 17?

options.text: You must not eat any fat or any blood.
options.note: Verse 17 states this prohibition as a permanent statute for all generations.

options.text: You must offer a peace offering every day.
options.note: No daily requirement for the peace offering is stated here; it was a voluntary offering.

options.text: Only priests may offer peace offerings.
options.note: The chapter describes any Israelite bringing this offering, not priests exclusively.

options.text: No lasting statute is given.
options.note: Verse 17 explicitly states a permanent statute.

quiz.q: What does the Hebrew word for peace offering, shelamim, relate to?

options.text: Shalom, meaning wholeness, well being, and peace.
options.note: The shared root points to restored relationship and completeness as the offering's meaning.

options.text: A word meaning silence or stillness.
options.note: This is not the root meaning connected to shelamim.

options.text: A word meaning fire or burning.
options.note: That concept relates more to olah, burnt offering, not shelamim.

options.text: The word has no connection to any other Hebrew concept.
options.note: Shelamim shares a clear root with shalom, peace and wholeness.

questions: The peace offering meant sharing an actual meal with joy in God's presence after atonement was made. Does your relationship with God feel more like a formal transaction or a genuine, joyful fellowship?
God claimed the fat, the richest part, before anything else was eaten. What is the best part of your time, money, or attention that you tend to keep for yourself rather than give to God first?

This offering could come from the herd, the flock, or a goat, showing that God welcomed worship from whatever a person had. Do you hold back from worship because you feel you do not have enough to offer?

The peace offering pictures the completed relationship, shalom, that reconciliation with God brings. Where in your life do you need to receive the peace Christ has already won rather than continuing to strive for it?
This meal anticipates the marriage supper of the Lamb, a feast still to come. How does looking forward to that future feast change the way you view struggles or losses in the present?

translationNotes.note: Peace offering translates shelamim, sharing its root with shalom; some translations render it fellowship offering to emphasize the shared meal that distinguishes it from the wholly burned offerings.

The entire fat tail cut off close to the backbone refers to the broad, fatty tail of certain Middle Eastern sheep breeds, considered a delicacy and therefore reserved specifically for God rather than human consumption.
This prohibition on eating fat and blood is called a permanent statute, chuqqat olam, distinguishing it from ceremonial regulations tied specifically to the tabernacle and priesthood.
